same_incident.label: Same underlying incident
same_incident.description: Both dockets are litigating the same November 1, 2024 traffic-shoulder encounter, so the same dashcam and the same officer conduct are the operative proof in each.

same_denial_challenged.label: Same agency action challenged
same_denial_challenged.description: Both dockets challenge the identical agency decision, so a ruling on that decision in one court is directly relevant in the other.

shared_predicate.label: Shared legal predicate
shared_predicate.description: Both dockets turn on the same threshold legal question, most often whether the encounter was a lawful arrest or a detention only.

stay_dependency.label: Stay dependency
stay_dependency.description: One docket is stayed pending resolution of the other, so the stayed matter's calendar is controlled by events on a different docket.

authority_dependency.label: Authority dependency
authority_dependency.description: A ruling or recommendation in one docket was relied on as reasoning in the other, so weakening the first weakens the second.

persuasive_authority.label: Persuasive authority cited
persuasive_authority.description: An order issued in one docket has been filed in the other as persuasive authority.

parallel_track.label: Parallel relief track
parallel_track.description: Both dockets seek overlapping relief on separate tracks, raising sequencing, abstention, and inconsistent-ruling risk.

damages_overlap.label: Overlapping damages claim
damages_overlap.description: The same economic loss is pleaded as damages in both dockets without an offset or reservation coordinating them.

disclosure_gap.label: Related-case disclosure gap
disclosure_gap.description: One docket's related-case disclosure omits a matter that the record shows is related.

clusters.label: CHP November 1, 2024 Encounter & U Visa Certification
clusters.thesis: Five live dockets in four courts — plus Matter 32 as the Meza-Gonzalez / CHP-cluster PDF home and Matter 33 as the Candelaria / DMV APS PDF home — run off one 62-minute traffic-shoulder encounter. The same dashcam, the same Penal Code § 849(b)(1) Detention Certificate, and the same April 20, 2026 certification denial are the operative proof across the cluster. That concentration is the portfolio's greatest source of leverage and its greatest source of exposure: a favorable finding on the shared record propagates across every member, and an adverse or inconsistent one does the same.

Both matters sat before the same district/magistrate pair (the shared DC-CSK suffix). Magistrate Judge Kim's June 15, 2026 Findings & Recommendations in Matter 7 cited Matter 1's April 20, 2026 dismissal recommendation as supporting grounds, and Matter 7's own theory depends on the 'lawful arrest' predicate that the Detention Certificate repudiates. Both matters were voluntarily dismissed without prejudice Aug. 15, 2026 before the District Judge ruled on either F&R — so the dependency was mooted rather than resolved; neither F&R was ever adopted or rejected. The relationship was one-directional: Matter 1's record shows no reciprocal citation to Matter 7.
The same February 20, 2025 – February 19, 2026 CDL suspension loss is claimed in both, unreserved.
Matter 20 claims approximately $112,000 in lost wages for the same one-year suspension window already claimed in Matter 1.

Matter 1 filed a Notice of Supplemental Authority on July 7, 2026 citing the Krishnan June 29, 2026 IFP order as persuasive authority against its own Findings & Recommendations — the argument being that a sister federal court screened a complaint on this same November 1, 2024 record and found it sufficient.
The same Krishnan IFP screening order is cited in Matter 7 as persuasive authority that a complaint resting on this record survives § 1915(e)(2) screening.

Both state-court dockets sit in Alameda Superior Court on the same encounter and the same certifying-agency conduct, on separate tracks — one stayed, one active — which creates a live risk of inconsistent state rulings on the identical record.

Both dockets challenge the April 20, 2026 U Visa certification denial arising from the same encounter — Matter 20 in state court, Matter 24 in federal court. Simultaneous challenges to one agency decision in two courts invite abstention, stay, or first-to-judgment arguments, and an adverse finding in either is available to the defense in the other.

exposures.label: Unreserved CDL lost-wage claim, now split across dismissed and successor dockets
exposures.detail: The one-year Class A CDL suspension loss was pleaded as damages in Matters 1, 2, 7, and 20 with no offset, reservation, or no-double-recovery language coordinating the dockets. Archived Matter 8, by contrast, expressly reserved consequential damages to the federal action — which is both the model to follow and evidence that the omission elsewhere is an inconsistency rather than a strategy. Matters 1, 2, and 7 were dismissed Aug. 15, 2026; Matters 32 and 33 already carry $0 placeholder rows in damages.js specifically to avoid double-counting against 1/2/7, but the underlying coordination problem persists — it just now runs between Matters 32, 33, and 20 instead.
exposures.remedy: Add reciprocal offset/no-double-recovery language to the damages allegations across Matters 32, 33, and 20, keying the primary recovery to one docket and reserving the rest.

exposures.label: Matters 1 and 7's F&Rs were mooted by dismissal, not resolved on the merits
exposures.detail: Matters 1 and 7 were voluntarily dismissed without prejudice Aug. 15, 2026, before District Judge Coggins ruled on either Findings & Recommendations — so neither F&R was ever adopted, but neither was reversed either; the adverse recommendations simply never became final. The Krishnan order remains a § 1915(e)(2) screening finding, not a merits ruling, still cited in Matter 20. The live question shifts from "how will Coggins rule" to whether Matters 32 and 33's fresh N.D. Cal. complaints draw the same magistrate/district scrutiny the E.D. Cal. dockets did, this time without an adverse F&R already on file.
exposures.remedy: Frame the Krishnan order as screening-stage only in future filings. Watch whether Matters 32/33 face renewed IFP screening or a motion to dismiss revisiting the same qualified-immunity ground the E.D. Cal. F&Rs relied on.

exposures.label: Matter 2's clock is keyed to Matter 1's appeal window
exposures.detail: Moot. Matter 2 was itself voluntarily dismissed without prejudice Aug. 15, 2026 rather than waiting out the stay, so there is no 'final resolution' date left to calendar and no risk of the stay outliving the evidence. The State/CHP defendant and the state-law claims that were exclusive to Matter 2 have no successor docket — see the two-dismissal-rule exposure and the timeline.json Nov. 1, 2026 entry for what replaces this risk.
exposures.remedy: Done — superseded by the Aug. 15, 2026 dismissal. No further calendaring needed on this item; see the new state-law-claims-gap exposure instead.

exposures.label: Matter 1's Aug. 15, 2026 dismissal may trip FRCP 41(a)(1)(B)'s two-dismissal rule
exposures.detail: Matter 13 (Newanforbi v. Urrea, cluster 2 — not in this cluster's matter list) was already dismissed by Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice on June 29, 2026, pleading the same five-day parole hold that Matter 1's complaint also pleads as a damages element. FRCP 41(a)(1)(B) provides that a second notice dismissal of an action 'based on or including the same claim' operates as an adjudication on the merits — i.e., WITH prejudice — regardless of how the notice is labeled. If a court finds that overlap sufficient, today's Aug. 15, 2026 Matter 1 dismissal is a merits dismissal, and Matter 32 (already on file in the N.D. Cal. since Aug. 10, 2026, pleading the identical Nov. 1, 2024 stop/search/arrest and the same five-day-hold damages theory) would be exposed to a res judicata defense. This was flagged as needing resolution before any notice was filed (see internal/docs/MATTER_01_FORUM_TRANSFER_ANALYSIS.md §3.2) and does not show as resolved in this record.
exposures.remedy: Get a definitive answer — ideally from counsel, given the stakes — on whether Matter 13's claim and Matter 1's claim are 'the same claim' for Rule 41(a)(1)(B) purposes before relying on Matter 32 as a clean refiling. If they are, consider whether Matter 32's five-day-hold damages component needs to be dropped or reframed to avoid res judicata exposure to the rest of the complaint.

exposures.label: Matter 2's state-law claims and the State/CHP defendant have no successor docket
exposures.detail: Matter 2's dismissal (Aug. 15, 2026) terminated the False Imprisonment, Battery, and Bane Act claims and the State of California/CHP defendant along with the rest of that action. Matter 32's N.D. Cal. complaint pleads only federal §1983 claims against Meza-Gonzalez and Melano individually — it does not name the State/CHP or assert any state-law theory. Unless this was an intentional abandonment, roughly $100,000–$300,000 of pleaded state-law exposure has no live vehicle, and the CCP §335.1 two-year backstop for those claims runs Nov. 1, 2026.
exposures.remedy: Confirm intentionally abandoned, or amend Matter 32 to add the state-law claims and the State/CHP defendant under 28 U.S.C. §1367 supplemental jurisdiction, or file a new state action — before Nov. 1, 2026.

exposures.label: Related-case disclosure is asymmetric between Matters 24 and 20
exposures.detail: Matter 20 named Matter 24 as the related federal action; Matter 24's original Complaint (Dkt. 1) did not name Matter 20. Plaintiff caught the omission independently and filed a First Amended Complaint with a concurrent Notice of Errata (Dkt. 10, 12; both Jul. 15, 2026) supplying the correction before any defendant raised it.
exposures.remedy: Done — First Amended Complaint and Notice of Errata filed Jul. 15, 2026 (Matter 24, Docs. 10 and 12).

exposures.label: The dispositive dashcam is not authenticated of record in every docket that relies on it
exposures.detail: The 62-minute recording is the proof that no alcohol odor was verbalized and that handcuffing preceded the parole-status disclosure. Multiple dockets argue from it, and Matter 33 now owns the transcript PDF, but the recording itself is not lodged and authenticated in each live docket, so an adverse evidentiary ruling in the docket where it is weakest would be cited against the others.
exposures.remedy: Lodge the recording with a declaration authenticating the timestamps in every matter that relies on it, and cite the same timestamp ranges consistently across filings.

exposures.label: One agency decision is being litigated in two courts at once
exposures.detail: The certification denial and the underlying encounter are before both Alameda Superior Court and the Northern District. Whichever court rules first supplies preclusion or persuasive material to the other, and a narrow adverse finding in the faster forum would travel.
exposures.remedy: Decide now which forum is the intended lead on the certification question and shape the filings so the other track expressly preserves rather than relitigates it.

foundation.label: The encounter itself
foundation.detail: November 1, 2024, approximately 00:54–01:57 a.m., eastbound I-580 dirt shoulder ~0.3 miles west of Isabel Avenue, Livermore. CHP Case No. RJ68845; CAD No. 241101GG0064. Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (#023295) and Jose Melano (#023054).

foundation.label: 62-minute dashcam recording
foundation.detail: 00:54:36–01:57:10. Establishes that no officer verbalized an alcohol odor, that the only liquid found was identified on tape as urine ('Is it water? No this is piss'), and that handcuffing at 01:11:16 preceded the 01:11:42 dispatch disclosure of parole status. Transcript PDF owned by Matter 33.
